paras: The arrest of railroad laborers near Davidson College took place on August 18, 1888, when a sheriff's posse and the Hornet's Nest Riflemen of Charlotte, North Carolina, overtook a traveling gang of Black railroad hands by special train and forced their surrender. Twenty-four or about thirty of the men were jailed in Charlotte on charges of theft, assault and firing on whites. Papers in several states carried the story, and one report said a crowd at the court house threatened to lynch the prisoners.

The gang was a railroad labor force moving its camp from Rock Hill, South Carolina, to Winston, North Carolina, after finishing work on the Charleston, Cincinnati and Chicago line. According to the Yorkville Enquirer, the men belonged to contractor J. T. Roddey of Rock Hill, who had a new contract on the Roanoke and Southern at Winston. Estimates of its size ranged from about eighty to nearly one hundred to 200 men. The gang passed through Charlotte on the evening of Friday, August 17, in carts, wagons and on foot.

On Saturday morning reports reached Charlotte that the men had entered gardens and watermelon patches, robbed chicken roosts, insulted white residents and fired on some whites, though no one was killed. A Charlotte special printed in the New-York Tribune added that they had held a man on a bridge for two hours and ruined the corn of Pink Henderson, a white farmer. The same report said one of the gang shot out an eye of George Andrews, called "a respectable colored man," and that men assaulted Mrs. Meares when she objected to their firing at her poultry.

Judge Oliver P. Meares issued a bench warrant, the sheriff summoned a posse, and Governor Scales was informed. A special train left the depot at 11:35 a.m. carrying Sheriff Cooper and thirty-eight members of the Hornet's Nest Riflemen, and picked up the chief of police's mounted posse along the way. The riflemen came out of the woods and surrounded the gang while the sheriff demanded unconditional surrender, and after a yell of defiance the men gave up without further resistance. Twenty-four were taken back to Charlotte, and the rest continued on their way.

At the Charlotte depot the riflemen formed a hollow square around the prisoners and marched them to the court house, followed by large crowds. The Atlanta Constitution's correspondent wrote that "threats of lynching made the prisoners tremble" during the excitement, a detail no other paper reported. After a preliminary examination the prisoners were committed to jail in default of $200 bail, with a hearing or trial set for Monday. No report of the Monday proceedings or their outcome appears in the coverage.

The story ran as a dated Charlotte dispatch of August 18 in two forms. The News and Courier special, carried by the Richmond Dispatch under the headline "An Invasion" and the deck "Lawlessness of South Carolina Negroes in North Carolina," described the men as having "a very savage appearance" and looking like "desperate characters." The Newberry Herald and News reprinted that text as "Taken by the Law" on August 23. A second Charlotte special appeared in the New-York Tribune as "Disorderly Railroad Hands" and in the Atlanta Constitution as "Lawless Negroes," with the subhead "The Militia Called Out to Arrest the Desperadoes."

The Yorkville Enquirer, in South Carolina, headed its version "Boisterous Railroad Men," named their employer, and wrote that they had passed through Charlotte "quietly and orderly" with "the usual equipage of railroad laborers," before repeating the wire's account of the night's depredations. The Asheville Citizen used the arrest for an editorial on the militia, calling it a "security against the alternative of mob law" and observing that there was "no violence, no bloodshed." All of the coverage came from white papers, and none gave an account from the laborers themselves.

The papers disagreed on how many men were arrested: twenty-four in the wire report and the Yorkville list, thirty in the Constitution, and "upwards of twenty" in the Asheville Citizen. They also differed on who called out the militia, naming the sheriff, a judge's bench warrant, or the mayor of Charlotte.

reader.title: Arrest of railroad laborers near Davidson College, 1888
bases: A sheriff, a mounted police posse and the Hornet's Nest Riflemen, acting on a bench warrant, captured a traveling gang of Black railroad laborers without bloodshed (A1, A2, A5); the only lynching element is one paper's report of crowd threats at the court house (A3).

No one was killed: the gang surrendered and was jailed (A1, A4), and the Asheville Citizen stressed there was 'no violence, no bloodshed' (A5). The Atlanta Constitution alone reports that a crowd's 'threats of lynching' frightened the prisoners at the court house (A3).

The News and Courier/Dispatch wire (A1, A4, A6) and a separate Charlotte special in the Tribune and Constitution (A2, A3) agree on the pursuit, surrender and jailing; the lynching threats rest on A3 alone.

accounts.label: News and Courier / Southern News Bureau wire
accounts.gist: A 'savage'-looking gang of nearly 100 from South Carolina raided gardens and roosts, insulted whites and fired on some; the sheriff's force overtook them by train and 24 surrendered and were jailed.

accounts.label: Charlotte special to the Tribune and Constitution
accounts.gist: A gang of 200 (or a laboring gang) of Three C's railroad hands held a man on a bridge, ruined a farmer's corn, shot out a Black man's eye and assaulted Mrs. Meares; a bench warrant followed and the prisoners faced lynching threats at the court house.

accounts.label: Yorkville Enquirer (Rock Hill side)
accounts.gist: The 80 men were J. T. Roddey's force and passed through Charlotte 'quietly and orderly' before the reported Friday-night depredations.

accounts.label: Asheville Citizen editorial
accounts.gist: The mayor sent the Rifles, upwards of twenty were brought back, and the episode showed an organized militia upholding the law without violence.

framing.detail: The Dispatch headlined 'An Invasion' and 'Lawlessness of South Carolina Negroes' and described the men as savage-looking 'desperate characters'.
The Constitution called the men 'Lawless Negroes' and 'Desperadoes' and reported the lynching threats without comment.
The Tribune's 'Disorderly Railroad Hands' gave a detailed list of alleged offences, including one against a Black man.
The Yorkville Enquirer's 'Boisterous Railroad Men' identified the employer and said the gang passed through Charlotte quietly, then repeated the wire account.
The Asheville Citizen praised the militia as a 'security against the alternative of mob law'.

conflicts.note: The papers do not agree; none was an eyewitness count.
The 24 names printed from the Charlotte Chronicle (A4) support 24.

info: The gang passed through Charlotte on Friday evening, Aug. 17, 1888; the pursuit and arrests took place on Saturday, Aug. 18.
The gang was overtaken on the Statesville road beyond Davidson College, near Mount Mourne; the alleged depredations occurred near Charlotte, Stonewall and Huntersville.

The arrested laborers, reported as 24 (A1, A4), 'thirty of the most guilty' (A3) or 'upwards of twenty' (A5); the Yorkville Enquirer printed 24 names from the Charlotte Chronicle: William Harris, John Grant, Wilson Mathison, Jule Harshaw, Jonas McIver, Scott Stinson, Ed. Jackson, Rachael Watson, Will Wilson, Frank Hargrave, John Smith, Will Henderson, Shep Blakely, Isaac Hoover, Horace Bryce, Wash Huntington, George Smith, Frank Brown, Jim Watts, Henry Hunt, Cardago Hayes, John Derby, Jim Brown, Tom Jones.

Accused of raiding gardens, watermelon patches and chicken roosts, insulting white residents, defying the authorities and firing on whites (A1, A4); of holding a man on a bridge, ruining Pink Henderson's corn, shooting out an eye of George Andrews, a Black man, and assaulting Mrs. Meares (A2, A3).
Sheriff Cooper, the Charlotte chief of police's mounted posse and the Hornet's Nest Riflemen, a militia company (A1, A4); at the court house, a large crowd that made threats of lynching (A3).
